strengths: Clear identification and formalization of component design as critical factor in Kronecker adapters, with motivating empirical evidence (Table 2)
Rigorous theoretical analysis grounded in Kronecker product SVD providing formal alignment guarantees (Theorem 3.2), with well-structured three-part proof
Novel training stabilization scaling factor λ ∈ Θ(1/√(r·r₂)) that provably equalizes gradient norms and effectively addresses optimization instability (Theorem 3.4, Figure 1)
Three interpretable design principles (maximize r₂, minimize r₁, constrain r ≥ r*) derived from theory and systematically validated empirically across ablations

Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple NLP domains (NLU, math reasoning, code generation), multiple model scales (T5-Base, LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), proper statistical reporting with means/stddev over 3 seeds, and verified computational efficiency
State-of-the-art results on mathematical reasoning (GSM8k: 56.71 vs 55.40 for LoRA-One) and strong results on code generation, with only 12.5% parameter overhead vs LoRA-One on NLU
Clear presentation with logical flow from motivation through theory to practice, informative figures (especially Figure 1 showing gradient stabilization), and useful practical guidelines
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis uses linear loss (Eq. 7) with Gaussian inputs while experiments employ nonlinear transformers with real data; conditions in Eq. 12 difficult to verify with standard Kaiming initialization, and breakdown conditions not discussed

Missing comparison with most closely related work MoKA (Sadeghi et al., 2025) in main results tables, dismissed due to 'computational overhead' without detailed justification despite being identified as most related

Heuristic parameter selection guidelines: determining r* for new tasks lacks principled methodology beyond empirical r* ∈ [2,8] boundary from one task; different tasks use vastly different configurations without clear decision procedure

Inconsistent ablation reporting: Tables 6-7 show only means without standard deviations in some ablations; HumanEval results have large std (~2.74), raising questions about statistical significance without formal significance tests

Theoretical justification gaps: why A⁽ⁱ⁾ random outperforms B⁽ⁱ⁾ random lacks explanation beyond empirical Table 8; relationship between theoretical initialization bounds and practical Kaiming initialization unexplored
Limited scope to NLP domain only; generalization to vision, audio, or other architectures unexplored; principles derived for transformers may not transfer
Modest improvements on several benchmarks: GLUE shows 87.30 vs 88.73 (1.43 pp gap to LoRA-One remains); improvements not always commensurate with added complexity of component design
Incomplete practical guidance: paper does not discuss when LoRA or alternatives might be preferable, or computational-accuracy tradeoffs making deployment decisions difficult

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in understanding component design for Kronecker adapters, providing systematic analysis where prior work treats design as fixed or heuristic
Derives three interpretable principles (small r₁, large r₂, moderate r) with empirical validation across single-epoch ablations, showing consistency between theory and practice
Achieves strong results on select benchmarks: state-of-the-art on GSM8k (56.71 vs LoRA-One 55.40) and second-best on HumanEval (24.59)
Provides practical contributions including a principled training stabilization strategy via scaling factor λ and verified computational efficiency (negligible overhead vs. LoRA)
Comprehensive experimental scope across diverse NLP tasks (GLUE, reasoning, code generation) and multiple model scales (T5, LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B)
weaknesses: Theoretical contribution is incremental: heavily adapted from Zhang et al. (2025), with Appendix B explicitly stating proofs are 'Adapted from Lemma C.5 in Zhang et al. (2025)'; core novelty is limited to Kronecker adapter context

Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 3.2 analyzes linear setting (Eq. 7), not actual nonlinear networks; initialization bounds (Eq. 12) depend on unknowns (σ₁(Ḡ₀), condition number κ) unverifiable in practice

Despite complex theoretical bounds, final practical guidelines are heuristic (r* ∈ [2,8], r₁ ∈ [2,4], α ∈ {16,64}) with no principled selection procedure; practitioners cannot use bounds to set hyperparameters

Inconsistent empirical improvements: CDKA underperforms on GLUE (87.30 vs. LoRA-One 88.73, -1.43pp regression unexplained); other gains are modest and within noise margins; creates doubt about when practitioners should use CDKA

Missing critical baseline comparisons: MoKA (Sadeghi et al., 2025) and MoKA-MoE (Yu et al., 2025) excluded citing 'computational overhead,' but Table 12 shows CDKA's overhead is negligible (~2%, same as KronA); these are the most relevant direct competitors for understanding component design

Severe experimental design limitations: all experiments use single-epoch training (unusual and unjustified), making generalization unclear; Tables 6-7 show near-identical performance across designs (56.71, 56.58, 56.38), contradicting claims about component design importance
Initialization strategy (Table 8) justified only empirically; no intuition provided; validation limited to single task configuration; fails to explain why A(i)←Kaiming, B(i)←0 is optimal

Hyperparameter selection is task/model dependent (Table 13: different α, different r₁, r₂, r per task/model) with no meta-procedure for new tasks; requires per-task experimentation, limiting practical impact

strengths: Novel theoretical framework connecting component design to subspace alignment via Kronecker SVD, with formal theorems deriving design principles
Strong empirical results: achieves SOTA on mathematical reasoning (56.71 vs 55.40 for LoRA-One) and second-best on code generation with comprehensive NLU evaluation
Practical contributions including training stabilization strategy (Theorem 3.4) with explicit scaling factor and clear hyperparameter guidelines under fixed budgets
Principled design principles derived from theory and validated empirically, contrasting with heuristic choices in prior work (KronA, MoKA)
Comprehensive experimental validation across three NLP domains with multiple baselines, proper statistical reporting (mean ± std dev over 3 seeds), and minimal computational overhead
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem, explicit principles, and effective organization
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis restricted to linear loss with isotropic Gaussian inputs; connection to non-linear neural networks is implicit and unexplored, limiting explanatory power
Limited validation of theoretical principles to single dataset (GSM8k) and model (LLaMA-2-7B); different task characteristics (NLU vs NLG) may exhibit different trends, weakening central claims

Missing comparisons with closely related methods MoKA and MoKA-MoE due to 'computational overhead' without characterizing actual trade-offs; makes it difficult to assess whether CDKA's design complexity is justified
Modest improvements on GLUE (average 2.92 points over KronA; CDKA underperforms LoRA-One on CoLA), undermining claims about 'fully unlocking potential'
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices (α=16, r*∈[2,8]) lack sensitivity analysis and principled justification for why these work across diverse settings
Inconsistency observation (Table 2) relies on single example; theoretical bounds in Theorem 3.2 are complex with many problem-dependent terms, limiting practical applicability for practitioners

strengths: Clear identification of under-explored design choices in Kronecker adapters with well-motivated theoretical analysis based on KSVD
Three interpretable design principles (small r₁, large r₂, moderate r) derived from Theorem 3.2 with consistent empirical validation across multiple tasks
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning NLU, NLG, and vision tasks with detailed ablations and robustness studies; efficient implementation with minimal computational overhead
Well-presented paper with practical guidelines for practitioners and clear hyperparameter specifications enabling reproducibility
Stabilization strategy (Theorem 3.4) is theoretically motivated and empirically effective for ensuring training stability
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis restricted to linear settings, severely limiting applicability to nonlinear deep networks; gap between alignment property and downstream task performance is loose and underexplored

Empirical improvements are modest and inconsistent: CDKA underperforms LoRA-One on GLUE (87.30% vs 88.73%), with improvements of 1-3% in most cases falling within standard deviation ranges, raising statistical significance concerns

Design guidelines inconsistent across tasks despite 'principled' framing: different r₁,r₂,r configurations used for different models/datasets; 'default' configuration still requires tuning, undermining universality claims
Excluded MoKA and MoKA-MoE baselines without quantitative justification of computational overhead; missing comparisons showing when Kronecker adapters are preferable to using more LoRA parameters

Hyperparameter α in scaling factor λ remains tunable across models (Table 16: α ∈ {16,32,64}), making solution not fully automatic; theoretical bounds contain many unknown constants making practical interpretation difficult
Complex theoretical bounds (Eq. 12) and time constraints (t* ≤ t^lin) difficult to interpret; some design choices lack conceptual justification (e.g., why random initialization for A and zero for B)

strengths: Clear problem motivation: identifies meaningful gap between theoretical promise and empirical performance of Kronecker adapters
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: tests across diverse NLP and CV tasks with multiple model sizes
Systematic ablation studies: Tables 3-7 thoroughly validate each design principle independently
Theoretical framework: Theorem 3.2 provides principled subspace alignment analysis grounded in Kronecker SVD
Practical stabilization mechanism: scaling factor λ addresses real training instability with theoretical justification (Theorem 3.4)
Extensive appendices: detailed proofs, additional experiments, and implementation details support reproducibility
weaknesses: Weak baseline comparisons: KronA set to r₁=r₂=64, r=1 without hyperparameter tuning; paper's ablations suggest better configurations exist, making KronA appear artificially weak
Unfair experimental setup: Table 9 compares CDKA (0.41M params) to LoRA-One (3.24M params) at vastly different budgets; CDKA actually underperforms on average (87.30 vs 88.73 on GLUE)
Missing critical baselines: MoKA and MoKA-MoE (most closely related recent work) excluded from experiments with weak justification

Limited novelty: three design principles are intuitive (small r₁ reduces complexity, large r₂ increases expressivity, r shows diminishing returns); hyperparameter analysis of existing method without fundamental new insights
Theory severely limited in scope: analysis restricted to linear loss (Eq. 7) with isotropic inputs and specific initialization; real networks are highly nonlinear, undermining theoretical claims

Theory-practice disconnect: subspace alignment metric (Eq. 11) doesn't clearly justify why design principles work; principles are validated empirically (Tables 3-5) rendering theory auxiliary rather than foundational
Marginal and inconsistent improvements: GLUE regression (87.30 vs 88.73), GSM8k +1.31 points, HumanEval ±2.74 variance, image classification +0.51 points; improvements often within error bars
Overclaimed results: 'state-of-the-art' claims unsupported by data (56.71 vs 54.04 with overlapping error bars); 'second-best code generation' actually worse than stated baseline

Additional hyperparameter tuning required: scaling factor α must be tuned per-model (α ∈ {16,32,64}); Table 17 shows α contributes significantly (55.62→56.71), suggesting component design alone insufficient
Complex, opaque bounds: initialization condition (Eq. 12) involves unknown constants and problem-dependent terms; practical relevance unclear
Incomplete presentation: code availability stated as 'available a' (incomplete sentence); KreshapeOperation notation difficult to parse
Limited failure analysis: no discussion of when CDKA fails, what task properties determine effectiveness, or generalization to untested domains

strengths: Clear problem motivation with empirical evidence (Table 2) that rank alone doesn't determine Kronecker adapter performance
Solid theoretical contribution via Kronecker SVD analyzing how component design affects subspace alignment with full fine-tuning
Three clear, actionable design principles derived from theory and validated empirically across multiple tables
Training stability analysis with principled scaling factor (Theorem 3.4) addressing practical optimization challenges
Comprehensive experiments across diverse settings: multiple architectures (T5, LLaMA, Qwen, CLIP), modalities (NLU, NLG, CV), and tasks with proper statistical reporting
Practical impact: makes Kronecker adapters competitive with SOTA PEFT while maintaining computational efficiency equal to LoRA
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, ablations, and promise of code release
Strong results on key benchmarks: SOTA on mathematical reasoning (56.71% vs 55.40%) and image classification (90.08% vs 89.57%)
weaknesses: Theory limited to linear settings with isotropic sub-Gaussian inputs; gap between linear analysis and nonlinear practice not rigorously bridged
Theoretical bounds (Eq. 12-13) contain unspecified universal constants and complex conditions, limiting practical interpretability and applicability
Mixed empirical results: worse than LoRA-One on GLUE NLU (87.30 vs 88.73), second-best on code generation, only SOTA on 2/4 task categories
Limited novelty: heavily adapts Zhang et al. (2025)'s alignment framework; contribution is more about understanding existing methods than proposing fundamentally new mechanisms
Initialization assumptions (Gaussian A, zero B) don't fully explain empirical findings on initialization sensitivity (Table 8)
Default configuration (r₁=2, r₂=8, r=4) appears empirically derived rather than theoretically justified, somewhat undermining theoretical guidance
Incomplete experimental comparisons: MoKA excluded due to computational overhead, preventing direct comparison on performance
Scope limited to transformer linear layers; unclear if principles generalize to other architectures
